terms.gloss: a table goods are sold from: a market stall
evidence: Lewis & Short s.v. mēnsa: a stand in the market for meat, vegetables, and the like (Suetonius)
terms.comment: The classical word for the table a seller sets out his goods on, and the money-changer his coins (Lewis & Short: “a market-stand for meat, vegetables, etc.”). The lexicon’s stalls for fruit, vegetables, and fish are built on it: see “fruit stall”.

terms.gloss: a booth, a stall, a shop built of boards
evidence: Mart. 7.61.10: Nunc Rōma est, nūper magna taberna fuit.
terms.comment: The general word for a booth or shop; where the stall is a covered booth rather than a table, taberna fits better. For a shop with walls, see “shop”.

phrases.latin: Abstulerat tōtam temerārius īnstitor urbem, inque suō nūllum līmine līmen erat.
phrases.english: The bold pedlar had taken over the whole city, and no doorway kept to its own doorstep.

phrases.latin: Ad mēnsam pōmāriam cōnstitimus, ubi pater māla ēmit.
phrases.english: We stopped at the fruit stall, where Dad bought apples.

phrases.latin: Quot mēnsae hodiē in forō sunt!
phrases.english: What a lot of stalls there are in the square today!

sources: Lewis & Short: mensa · Lewis & Short: taberna
